questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify density-dependent regulation from per-plant damage data.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-101: In a garden, aphid colonies grow slowly when sparse but each plant is stripped bare when colonies are dense. Which regulation is operating here?

options.text: Density-dependent regulation, because the damage per plant rises as the colony grows denser on the same resources
Density-independent regulation, because a cold snap during the season killed the colonies before they filled the plants
options.misconception: attributes the slow growth to weather rather than crowding

options.text: Predator regulation, because the aphids were eaten by ladybirds and spiders once colonies became dense
options.misconception: assumes the regulator must be a predator rather than a resource

options.text: No regulation occurred, because the colonies still persisted after the season ended and nothing stopped them
options.misconception: believes regulation requires the population to die out completely

questions.explanation: Damage per plant rose as colonies crowded the same plants, the signature of density-dependent regulation. Weather, predators alone, and colony survival cannot explain why per-plant damage tracked crowding.
questions.hint: Check whether per-individual effects change with crowding.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish delayed density dependence from immediate control.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-102: A fishery ticket notes that the cod recruitment in a given year is set by the spawning biomass two years earlier. What kind of dependence does this show?

options.text: Immediate density dependence, because spawners and recruits are measured in the same fishing season
options.misconception: conflates same-season measurement with a causal link

options.text: Delayed density dependence, because the spawning biomass affects recruitment two years later rather than at once
Density-independent regulation, because recruitment was driven by ocean temperature rather than by biomass
options.misconception: dismisses any biomass link because temperature also varies

options.text: Positive feedback, because larger spawning stocks always produce proportionally larger year classes
options.misconception: reads a lagged link as a positive feedback loop

questions.explanation: Biomass influences a later life stage two years downstream, so the dependence is lagged. Same-season measurement does not remove the lag, and temperature does not exclude a biomass link.
questions.hint: Check how many years separate cause and response.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Solve the continuous growth rate from an exponential model fit.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-103: A colleague fits N(t) = N0 e^(rt) to a colony with 1000 cells at t = 0 and 2718 cells at t = 10 years. What per-year continuous rate r does the model imply?
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives r = ln(2718/1000)/10 = ln(2.718)/10, about 0.10 per year. Dividing the ratio by ten without a logarithm, or treating growth as linear, misses the model's assumption.
questions.hint: Take a natural logarithm of the population ratio.

questions.topic: Per-capita rate of increase from births and deaths
questions.learningObjective: Build a per-capita rate of increase from breeding and loss counts.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-104: A ticket asks how to compute the per-capita rate of increase for a shorebird colony with 90 nests, 120 fledglings produced and 35 adults lost.

options.text: Divide fledglings by nests and ignore the losses, since losses are already reflected in later counts
options.misconception: ignores deaths because later counts already include them

options.text: Add fledglings and losses and divide by nests, since every outcome should be counted
options.misconception: adds losses to gains instead of subtracting them

options.text: Subtract losses from fledglings and divide by nests: (120 - 35) / 90 gives 0.944 per nest per year
Divide the 35 losses by 120 fledglings, since mortality is best expressed per surviving bird
options.misconception: expresses mortality per fledgling instead of per adult

questions.explanation: Per-capita rate of increase is (births - deaths) divided by population: (120 - 35) / 90 = 0.944 per nest per year. Ignoring deaths, adding them to births, or dividing by fledglings corrupt the net rate.
questions.hint: Net change first, then divide by the population.

questions.explanation: Two counts five years apart give lambda = (3000/250)^(1/5) = 12^0.2 = 1.64 per year. Dividing the counts, or taking the wrong root, treats compound growth as a straight line.
questions.hint: Raise the population ratio to the power one over five.

questions.stem: Ticket TKT-106: A dashboard tabulates the ratio of each year to the previous one: 0.9, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4. What does the trend say about the finite rate of increase?

options.text: The finite rate of increase is falling each year, since the ratios themselves decline over the four years
options.misconception: mistakes a rising ratio series for a falling growth rate

options.text: The population is shrinking every year, because a ratio below one appears in the first row of the table
options.misconception: reads one sub-unity ratio as the whole trend

options.text: The population must be near carrying capacity, because ratios above one always mean density-dependent control
options.misconception: assumes growth above one implies density-dependent regulation

options.text: The finite rate of increase is rising through the period, since each year's ratio exceeds the one before it

questions.explanation: Each year's finite rate is the ratio of that year to the last, and here the ratios climb from 0.9 to 1.4, so the multiplier is rising. The one sub-unity value describes only the first year.

questions.topic: Logistic rate of increase at a stated size
questions.learningObjective: Design a plan that estimates logistic growth parameters from field data.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-107: Design a plan that estimates the logistic growth rate dN/dt of a reindeer herd at a stated herd size N, and checks it against the predicted K and r.

answer.exemplar: Survey the herd at regular intervals, record the population size and count calves born each year, then estimate the per-capita rate of increase r = (births - deaths)/N for several herd sizes. Fit a logistic curve to those size and growth-rate pairs by least squares to recover estimates of the carrying capacity K and the intrinsic rate r, and check whether the fitted rN(1 - N/K) values match the observed per-capita growth at each size within the survey error.

questions.explanation: A good design estimates per-capita growth at several herd sizes, since only that relationship reveals both K and r. One size cannot separate the parameters, and a single census misses births and deaths.
questions.hint: Sample growth rate at many herd sizes, not one.

questions.stem: Ticket TKT-108: A colleague labels a drought-driven crash of a grasshopper population as density-dependent because the crash was severe, and the population was large beforehand. Identify the flaw.

options.text: Severity is not the test; the key is whether the drought's effect changes with how crowded the population was
The analysis is fine, because any event that reduces a population must be density-dependent by definition
options.misconception: assumes all population declines must be density-dependent

options.text: The flaw is that the population was counted at the wrong time of year, and no density effect can be shown at all
options.misconception: claims seasonal timing of the count rules out any density effect

options.text: The flaw is that droughts are rare, so the data cannot support any claim about population regulation
options.misconception: says rare events can never explain a population decline

questions.explanation: The test is whether the per-individual effect changes with density, not how severe the effect is. A drought crash acts the same way at any crowding level, so labelling it density-dependent misreads the cause.

questions.stem: Ticket TKT-109: A pond survey records 120 births and 180 deaths in a year among 1600 fish at peak density. What is the per-capita rate of increase per fish per year?

options.misconception: believes crowding changes survival immediately in the same season

options.text: Delayed density dependence, because crowding changes the host trees only after a lag of several years

questions.stem: Ticket TKT-111: A colony assumed to grow exponentially with a doubling time of 3 years starts at 500 cells. How many cells are expected after 12 years?

questions.learningObjective: Relate a continuous growth rate to a yearly multiplier.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-114: A ticket asks how lambda relates to the intrinsic rate r when a population is checked once per year.

options.text: Lambda equals r, because both describe growth and both are measured per year
options.misconception: treats a multiplier and a continuous rate as identical

options.text: Lambda is the inverse of r, because population declines as the rate rises
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between rate and multiplier

Lambda equals one plus r squared, because compounding works only for squared rates

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study separating food competition from predation.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-117: Outline a field study that would show whether competition for food, rather than predation, regulates the colony of ground squirrels on a vacant lot.

answer.exemplar: Set up plots with three treatments: natural density, density reduced by removing a fixed number of squirrels, and density increased by adding squirrels from another lot, all with food supplied identically. Monitor per-capita survival, reproduction and body condition for two breeding seasons, and use the food-supplied treatment to separate food limitation from predation. If per-capita reproduction and survival fall as density rises even where predators are excluded, food competition is the regulatory mechanism; if they hold steady, predation is doing the regulating.

questions.explanation: Manipulating density while holding other causes constant ties changes in per-capita rate to the intended mechanism. Food-supplied and predator-excluded treatments separate competition from predation.
questions.hint: Manipulate density and hold other causes constant.

options.text: The flaw is that the note treated the crash as density-independent just because the timing differed
options.misconception: treats any time lag as proof of independence

questions.explanation: A lag between crowding and response is the signature of delayed density dependence, so a crash two years later still implicates density. Reading the lag as proof crowding was uninvolved is the error.
questions.hint: A lag is not the same as no effect.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test distinguishing exponential from logistic growth.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-127: Design an experiment that tests whether a yeast colony grows exponentially or instead follows a logistic curve as space runs out.

answer.exemplar: Grow the yeast in a series of identical tubes at constant temperature and record the population every few hours for long enough to approach a plateau, while also varying the initial inoculum across treatments. Fit both an exponential model N = N0 e^(rt) and a logistic model to the full time series and compare the fits, for example by residuals and by the estimated carrying capacity. A rising per-capita rate that later falls toward zero, or a consistent plateau across inocula, supports logistic rather than exponential growth.

questions.explanation: The test must run long enough to see whether growth slows, since exponential and logistic curves agree early on. Fitting both models to one long series at several starting densities exposes the downturn.
questions.hint: Run the culture long enough for growth to slow.

200 animals per year, because (1600 - 400) / 5 divides the net change by the number of years
options.misconception: divides the net change by time and calls it a growth rate

options.text: 300 animals per year, because the three intervals of growth between four data points average out
options.misconception: averages interval gains as if the growth were linear

options.text: 1.2 animals per year, because the population quadrupled over the period and quadruples split evenly
options.misconception: splits a fourfold gain evenly across the years

questions.explanation: Growth over five years compounds, so the per-year multiplier is the fifth root of 1600/400 = 4, giving 1.149. Linear averaging of the net change ignores compounding.

questions.stem: Ticket TKT-137: Design a survey plan that yields reliable population counts five years apart so that the growth rate between the two dates can be estimated.

answer.exemplar: Mark and tag a random sample of animals during the first census, record the number of marks released and the number of marked animals recaptured in the same area at the second census five years later, and estimate each population size with the standard mark-recapture formula. questions.learningObjective: Design a monitoring plan that estimates logistic parameters.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-147: Design a monitoring plan that estimates the logistic growth rate of a recovering woodland bird population at several population sizes.

answer.exemplar: Count breeding adults in a set of fixed study plots every year for at least five years, and record both the number of breeding pairs and the number of young fledged per plot, so that the per-capita rate of increase can be calculated for each plot separately. Then fit a logistic curve to the set of per-capita growth rates against plot population size, using the fitted curve to estimate the carrying capacity and the intrinsic rate. Repeat across plots of different sizes and check that the estimated parameters agree across years and plots before reporting them.

questions.explanation: Logistic parameters are recoverable only if growth rates are measured at many sizes, since one size leaves K and r confounded. Recording young produced with adult counts supplies births and deaths.
questions.hint: Measure growth rates at several population sizes.

questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment separating two density-dependent mechanisms.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-157: Design an experiment that separates competition for food from waste accumulation as the density-dependent regulator of a caged mouse colony.

answer.exemplar: Run three treatment groups at the same high density: one with food replaced and waste removed as soon as it accumulates, one with food replaced but waste left in place, and one with food limited but waste removed daily. Keep all other conditions identical and record per-capita survival, time to first litter, litter size and body weight over several litters. If the waste-removal group matches the clean group while the food-limited group shows lower per-capita reproduction, then waste accumulation is the regulatory factor; if only the food-limited group is depressed, competition for food is the regulator.

questions.explanation: The design must vary one suspected mechanism at a time while holding density fixed, so differences can be attributed. Lowering density alone cannot separate food competition from waste build-up.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a lagged measurement is appropriate.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-158: A ticket says a report wrongly measured the response of a snail colony to crowding by counting adults three years after the crowding peak, and calls the measurement wrong. What is the best response?

options.text: The report is right to object, because delayed density dependence cannot be measured at all
options.misconception: believes lagged effects cannot be observed

options.text: Measuring adults three years later is right, because the delayed effect of crowding appears in the adults that survived
The report is right to object, because adult counts are less informative than counting empty shells
options.misconception: prefers a different indicator over the same effect

options.text: The report is right to object, because density should be recorded on the same day as the adult counts
options.misconception: insists on same-day density measurement

questions.explanation: Delayed density dependence means crowding's effect appears later, so counting adults three years on is the correct window. Demanding same-day measurement, or calling lagged effects unobservable, rules out the effect.
questions.hint: The lag is exactly what makes later counting correct.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption of exponential growth that fails in field populations.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-159: A ticket asks which assumption an exponential growth model makes that most often fails in a real field population.

options.text: That the starting population size is known exactly, which is hard because counts are estimates
options.misconception: blames counting error rather than the growth assumption

options.text: That births and deaths happen at exactly the same moment, so growth can be modelled smoothly
options.misconception: invents a synchrony assumption as the key flaw

options.text: That a constant per-capita rate holds over time, which breaks down as resources limit the population
That the model applies only to very large populations, since small ones behave differently
options.misconception: invents a size threshold for the model's validity

questions.explanation: An exponential model assumes a constant per-capita rate, so it predicts growth that continues and accelerates in percentage terms. In field populations crowding and resource limits usually push that rate down.
questions.hint: Ask what the model holds constant over time.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Per-capita rate of increase from births and deaths
questions.learningObjective: Compute a per-capita rate of increase from birth and death counts.
questions.stem: Ticket TKT-160: A colony of 400 animals produced 180 young and lost 40 adults over one year. What is the per-capita rate of increase per animal per year?
questions.explanation: Per-capita rate of increase is (births - deaths) divided by population: (180 - 40) / 400 = 0.35 per animal per year. Adding the losses to the births, or dividing births alone by the population, drops a required quantity.
questions.hint: Net births first, then divide by population.
